questions.q: What formally describes the structure of a SOAP service, in a way REST has no equivalent for?
options: A cookie
A WSDL (Web Services Description Language) contract document
An HTML page
A CSV schema file
questions.explain: SOAP services are described by a formal WSDL contract, which clients can use to generate strongly-typed code. REST has no equivalent formal contract file.

questions.q: In REST terms, what is a 'resource'?
options: The HTTP verb used in a request
The access token sent in the Authorization header
The 'noun' a URL addresses — such as an Account record or a query result
The WSDL file describing the API
questions.explain: A resource is the thing being acted on — the noun — while the HTTP verb (GET, POST, PATCH, DELETE) is the action taken on it.

questions.q: Why does every single REST API call need its own authentication token, even the tenth call in a row from the same client?
options: Because REST is a stateless protocol — the server retains no memory of previous requests, so each one must be fully self-contained
Because tokens expire after exactly one call
Because Salesforce requires a new token for every HTTP verb
Because SOAP calls don't need authentication, only REST calls do
questions.explain: Statelessness means the server doesn't remember prior requests, so authentication (and everything else the server needs) has to be included on every call, not just the first.

questions.q: An overnight job needs to import 500,000 historical records once a month. Based on this lesson, should this integration be synchronous or asynchronous?
options: Synchronous, because historical data should always be loaded instantly
It doesn't matter, since SOAP and REST behave identically either way
Synchronous, because asynchronous calls are only valid for SOAP APIs
Asynchronous — a job this large should be submitted and processed in the background rather than making the caller wait for an immediate response
questions.explain: Work at this scale takes real time to process and would time out or be impractical as a blocking synchronous call — this is exactly the use case asynchronous processing (like Bulk API 2.0) is designed for.

questions.q: Which pair of HTTP verbs, per this lesson's REST convention, map to 'create' and 'delete'?
options: POST and DELETE
GET and PATCH
DELETE and POST
PATCH and GET
questions.explain: POST conventionally creates a new resource, and DELETE removes one — GET reads, and PATCH partially updates.
